verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to YHWH, for [he is] good, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the LORD. Say it aloud, and say why: he is good. His faithful love does not run out. It lasts as long as time itself.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a stock liturgical opening (compare 106:1, 118:1, 136:1, 1 Chr 16:34), and the actors should hear it as a call from a crowd gathered in the courtyard of the temple, not as a private prayer. The verb hodu is a command to confess aloud, so that thanks is spoken in public with the sacrifice of thanksgiving (todah) it goes with. The KJV's 'his mercy endureth for ever' is the most familiar line in English worship, and it is both archaic and slightly off: chesed is not pity for the weak but loyalty inside a bond, what a lord owes his people and a kinsman owes his kin. 'Mercy' makes it sound like a favour; the Hebrew makes it a commitment he keeps. 'For ever' translates le'olam, literally 'to the age', time as far as the eye can see.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty: the faithful commitment of one party in a bond. KJV 'mercy' and ASV 'lovingkindness' each catch only a part; the word binds goodness to a promise.

Hiphil imperative of yadah: to confess, acknowledge, thank in public speech. The same root recurs in the refrain of vv.8, 15, 21, 31 (yodu), so the repeated English 'give thanks' should be kept throughout.

verses.translation_literal: Let them say, the redeemed of YHWH, whom he redeemed from the hand of [the] adversary,
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them say it, the ones the LORD bought back, the ones he pulled out of the grip of the enemy.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the psalm names its choir: the ge'ulim, 'the redeemed'. The verb ga'al belongs to family law. The go'el was the kinsman who bought back a relative sold into debt or slavery, or who avenged him. So the singers are not merely rescued; they have a relative who paid. 'The hand of the adversary' is physical: a hand that holds a wrist. The KJV's 'say so' adds a 'so' that is not in the Hebrew, and 'enemy' loses the pun with tzar, 'narrow' (v.6 uses the same word, batzar, 'in the narrow place', which the English versions scatter into 'trouble', 'adversity' and 'distress'). Ibn Ezra reads the whole psalm as the speech of these redeemed ones.

philological_notes.note: Passive participle of ga'al, redeem: the kinsman's act of buying someone back. The same root is repeated in 'whom he redeemed' (ge'alam).
Both 'adversary' and, as an adjective, 'narrow'. Radak glosses it as 'tzarah', trouble. The sound returns in batzar (v.6) and metzukot (v.6, 13, 19, 28).

verses.translation_literal: And from [the] lands he gathered them, from [the] east and from [the] west, from [the] north and from [the] sea.
verses.translation_dramatic: And out of the lands he gathered them: from the sunrise and from the sunset, from the north, and from the sea.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse widens the stage from one rescued man to a people scattered across the map, and it is the line that made later readers hear the psalm as a return from exile (Targum, Meiri, Malbim). The surprise is the last word. Every English version in the packet except YLT writes 'from the south', because four compass points sound complete. The Hebrew says umiyam, 'and from the sea', and the sea is itself a direction: for a Judean standing in Jerusalem the Mediterranean is the west, so 'sea' next to 'west' needs explaining. Ibn Ezra and Radak conclude that the south was left out because the heat made it thinly settled, and read 'sea' as the lands across the water; Metzudat David reads 'the islands of the sea'. Isaiah 49:12 has the same oddity ('from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Sinim'), so the list is not a simple compass. The KJV harmonized by quietly deleting an unusual word. The actors should hear a speaker running out of directions, and then adding the one that looks like the end of the earth.

philological_notes.note: 'And from the sea.' Not 'south'. Commentators understand it as the seafaring lands or islands, or as a fourth direction after the three land directions; the south is absent because it was thinly settled.
Piel of qabatz, gather: the verb of ingathering used for the return of scattered Israel.

verses.translation_literal: They wandered in the wilderness, in [a] wasteland, [a] road; [a] city of dwelling they did not find.
verses.translation_dramatic: They wandered in the wilderness, in the empty waste, on a road that went nowhere. A city to live in, they never found one.
verses.directors_commentary: Here begins the first of the four portraits (travellers in the desert, prisoners, the sick, sailors). The scene is the caravan route: merchants carrying goods between lands, as Radak says, trusting a track that wind and sand can erase. The Hebrew piles up desolation: midbar (open steppe, pasture land), then yeshimon, the true wasteland, then derekh, a road you cannot see. The KJV's 'solitary way' is a guess; 'solitary' is not what yeshimon means, and ASV's 'desert way' is closer. The lack is stated in terms of town life, not of food: 'a city of dwelling'. For a farmer or trader of the ancient Near East the city is the place with walls, water, a market and law, the only protection from raiders and thirst. The line to land in performance is the last, with the negative at the very end of the verse: 'did not find'.

philological_notes.note: Yeshimon: a desolate waste, harsher than midbar. The sense of 'solitary' in the KJV is not in the word. Ibn Ezra says he explained it elsewhere; Malbim ranks it as emptier than the wilderness.
A city of dwelling, i.e. an inhabited town. The phrase returns in v.7 and v.36 as the answer to this lack, and the verb yashav also begins v.10.

verses.translation_literal: Hungry, also thirsty, their life in them kept wrapping itself.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hungry, and thirsty too. The life inside them folded in on itself and began to go dark.
verses.directors_commentary: Two short adjectives, then the failing body. The water skins and bread, which Radak says travellers carried for the number of days between towns, ran out because the lost road made the journey longer. Nefesh is the word the English Bible renders 'soul', and in the KJV 'their soul fainted in them' sounds like a spiritual crisis. In Hebrew the nefesh is the throat, the breath and appetite, the whole needing creature, and it is physical thirst that is described (v.9 will use the same word for the longing throat). The verb tit'attaf is 'to wrap oneself, to be covered over', the same verb used for the swooning at Lamentations 2:12, so the picture is of a person folding into a faint, as Metzudat David says, 'wrapped up on himself'. The KJV 'fainted' is acceptable; the BBE paraphrase loses the verb entirely.

philological_notes.note: The living, needing person: throat, appetite and breath together. 'Soul' in the KJV gives it too spiritual a tone.
Hithpael of 'atav: to wrap oneself, to be enveloped, hence to grow faint or swoon. Ibn Ezra compares it to 'those wrapped in hunger'.

token_glosses.gloss: it kept wrapping itself, grew faint

verses.translation_literal: And they cried out to YHWH in the straits to them; from their narrow places he would deliver them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they cried out to the LORD, there in the tight place. Out of their narrow places he pulled them free.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the first appearance of the psalm's turn (it returns in vv.13, 19 and 28). The shape is always the same: pressure, an outcry, rescue. The cry is tza'aq, the loud call of someone with no other resource; Malbim notes that the psalmist uses the stronger tza'aq for desert and sea, where death is near, and the milder za'aq (vv.13, 19) for prison and illness. The sound game is lost in the KJV's 'trouble' and 'distresses': batzar and mimetzukotehem both come from the idea of being squeezed into a narrow space. The Hebrew says it twice, 'in the narrow place' and 'from their narrow places', and the English should too. The rescue verb, hitzil, is 'to snatch out', not the weaker 'save'. The KJV 'he delivered' fixes the tense in the past; the imperfect yatzilem has the feel of 'this is what he does'.

philological_notes.note: 'In the narrow place': the same root as tzar, 'adversary' (v.2) and metzukot, 'straits'. The KJV 'trouble' loses the image of confinement.
From metzuqah, a tight spot or pressure. Metzudat Zion ties it to tzuqah, 'trouble'. It is plural: many straits, each answered.
Cried out. In vv.6 and 28 (desert and sea) the verb is tza'aq, in vv.13 and 19 it is za'aq; Malbim reads the stronger verb as marking the greater danger.

verses.translation_literal: And he made them tread by a straight way, to go to a city of dwelling.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he set their feet on a road that ran straight, and it led them to a city where people live.
verses.directors_commentary: The rescue answers the loss of verse 4 word for word, and Ibn Ezra sees it: 'they wandered' becomes 'he made them tread', and 'a city of dwelling they did not find' becomes 'to go to a city of dwelling'. Ta'u (wandered) is the opposite of yesharah (straight, level). The verb vayadrikhem is the causative of darakh, 'to tread': God puts them on the road step by step, the way a shepherd or a herald walks ahead of people. The KJV 'led them forth by the right way' is fine in sense, but 'right' (moral) is not 'straight'; the Hebrew asks the actors to hear a level, even road after a trackless sand. The Targum adds Jerusalem here, 'to Jerusalem, the city of habitation', which shows how early the psalm was read as a return to Zion.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of darakh: he made them tread, set them walking. Rashi glosses it as 'led them'; Metzudat David as 'put it in their heart to tread the straight way'.
A straight, level road, the reverse of the lost track of v.4 (Ibn Ezra: 'the opposite of ta'u').

verses.translation_literal: Let them give thanks to YHWH [for] his covenant loyalty, and [for] his wonders to the sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them give thanks to the LORD for his faithful love, for the wonders he works among the children of men.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the refrain (repeated at vv.15, 21, 31), and the performer should deliver it the same way each time, a little louder, like a congregation's response. The grammar is a jussive: 'let them give thanks'. The KJV's 'Oh that men would praise' makes it a wistful wish, as if no one does; the Hebrew is a summons to the people just described. 'Sons of Adam', bene adam, means humankind, not Israel only; the wonders (nifla'ot, things that are beyond what is expected) are for all people. Malbim's remark is useful for the actors: the miracle seems small to God, but it is a wonder from the human side, because the food and the road arrive where there was none. KJV 'for his goodness' replaces chesed, loyalty, with a general moral quality.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle of pala: things set apart, beyond ordinary expectation. 'Wonders' is nearer than the KJV's 'wonderful works'.
'To the sons of Adam': to humankind, not to Israel alone. The phrase returns in each refrain.

verses.translation_literal: For he has satisfied a longing throat, and a hungry throat he has filled [with] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he has given the parched throat its fill, and the starving one he has loaded with good things.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason for the thanks is spoken in two parallel halves, each with a nefesh: the longing one and the hungry one. In English 'soul' again blurs it; in Hebrew the word is the throat, the open mouth of need, and the verse is about water and bread. The verbs are a pair: hisbia' (he has made sated) and mile' (he has filled), and 'good' (tov) ends the line, echoing the 'he is good' that opened the psalm. So the audience hears the claim of verse 1 proved with a meal. Shoqeqah is a rare form for 'longing, rushing about', Meiri and Radak explain it from the root shuq (compare the surge in Joel 2:9 and Isaiah 29:8), and it describes the way a thirsty creature rushes at water. The KJV 'satisfieth' puts it in the present; the verbs here are perfect (completed), a rescue that has already happened.

philological_notes.note: Feminine participle meaning 'longing, rushing, eager'. Meiri and Radak derive it from shuq, with the final radical doubled; Metzudat Zion compares Isaiah 29:8, 'his throat is longing'.
Throat, appetite, the living person in need. Both halves of the verse use it, so keep the repetition.

verses.translation_literal: Those who sit [in] darkness and deep darkness, prisoners of affliction and iron.
verses.translation_dramatic: And some sat in the dark, in the deepest dark, prisoners held by misery and by iron.
verses.directors_commentary: The second portrait, with no verb of its own: just a list of people in a cell. 'Those who sit' (yoshvei) is the sitting of an inmate; the same verb gave us 'city of dwelling' (moshav), so those who could not find a place to live now live in the dark. Tzalmavet is traditionally read 'shadow of death' (tzel + mavet), which is how the KJV renders it, and Metzudat Zion follows that reading; many modern scholars take it as an old word for 'deep darkness' with no 'death' in it at all. The literal layer keeps 'deep darkness'. 'Iron' is concrete: ankle shackles, as Radak says, an ordinary way of holding a prisoner (compare Ps 105:18, of Joseph). The Targum applies the verse to Zedekiah and the leaders of Israel in Babylon, a historical reading the actors need not adopt. The KJV 'being bound in affliction' makes the Hebrew's two nouns into a participle phrase; the Hebrew says the prisoners belong to affliction and to iron.

philological_notes.note: Traditionally 'shadow of death' (tzel + mavet; Metzudat Zion: 'the shadow of death, as the darkness of the grave'). Modern lexica often read 'deep darkness', as an intensive of tzelem. I gave 'deep darkness' in the literal layer.
Prisoners, 'the bound ones'. Rashi applies this verse to those who come out of prison and must give thanks.
Affliction, humbling. Radak reads it as cords or ties that torment (from 'anah); Meiri as 'torments'.

verses.translation_literal: For they rebelled [against] the words of God, and the counsel of the Most High they spurned.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they had defied the words of God, and had waved aside the counsel of the Most High.
verses.directors_commentary: Unlike the desert travellers, whose trouble has no cause given, the prisoners have a charge against them, and it is stated in the word order: first 'rebelled' (himru, from the root of marah, 'to be bitter, stubborn'), and at the end 'spurned' (na'atzu), with 'the words of God' and 'the counsel of the Most High' in the middle as a pair. Radak says imrei El are the commandments given to all humankind, not to Israel alone, which fits the 'sons of Adam' of the refrain. Elyon, 'Most High', is the old title used in speech to or about the God above the gods of the nations, and here it carries the sense of a ruler whose advice was ignored, as a king's counsel might be by a headstrong prince. The KJV 'contemned' means 'despised' and is now obscure, and BBE's 'laws' and 'gave no thought' turn a word of contempt into a word of neglect. The Hebrew verb is 'to treat as nothing, to reject with scorn'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of marah: to be rebellious, to defy. Metzudat Zion ties it to meri, rebellion. Ibn Ezra notes it is close in sense to the Qal.
To spurn, to treat with contempt (Metzudat Zion: 'an expression of scorn'). The KJV 'contemned' is the archaic equivalent.
'Most High', an ancient divine title, here used of YHWH as the highest authority.

verses.translation_literal: And he humbled their heart with labour; they stumbled, and there was no helper.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he broke their pride with hard labour. They stumbled and went down, and there was no one to lift them.
verses.directors_commentary: The consequence arrives with a change of subject: God is the one who vayakhna, 'brought low', their heart, and then the grammar turns to 'they' as they stumble. Kana' means to make someone bow, to subdue; the heart (lev) is the seat of will and pride in Hebrew, so what is humbled is the stubborn will of verse 11, and 'amal, 'labour', is the toil of forced work and hardship (Ibn Ezra: slaves worked 'with crushing labour'; Radak: the toil of captivity). The KJV 'brought down their heart' is acceptable; ASV and Webster keep it, and BBE's 'weighted down with grief' substitutes a feeling for the labour. 'They stumbled' (kashelu) is the verb of the foot that gives way, and the closing phrase, ve'ein ozer, 'and there was no helper', sets the ground for the next verse's cry: when no human helper is left, the only one left is the one they had spurned. The KJV 'fell down' is a fair rendering; the tone should be sparse, with a pause before 'no helper'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of kana': to subdue, bring low. God is the subject; the heart is the object.
With toil, trouble: hard labour. Ibn Ezra reads it as the forced labour of captors; Radak as the hardship of captivity.
They stumbled, tottered. Radak specifies the setting as captivity; Metzudat David as the trouble in prison.

verses.translation_literal: And they cried out to YHWH in the distress to them; from their troubles he saved them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they cried out. Out of the narrow place, with nothing else left in them, they cried to the LORD. And out of those tight, pressing troubles he saved them.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the refrain that returns four times in the psalm, the hinge on which every one of the four scenes turns. Notice the shape of the Hebrew: the cry and the rescue are two short lines with nothing between them, no delay and no bargaining. The KJV's 'in their trouble… out of their distresses' is accurate but blurs the root play: tsar ('distress', literally a tight, narrow place) in the first half and metsuqot ('troubles', from the root tsuq, 'to press, to squeeze') in the second both belong to the family of narrowness. The people are squeezed, and God brings them out into room. Say 'tight place' and 'squeezes' and the actors will find the physical image. Also note the verb: zaʿaq is the cry of one who is wronged or in danger, a shout aimed at someone who can hear, not a prayer composed in calm. Ibn Ezra observes that 'he saved them' is mentioned here because they were in the hand of their enemies.

philological_notes.note: 'In the tight place, in distress'; the root means to bind or press in, and its noun forms are the standard Hebrew words for trouble. It pairs with metsuqot ('squeezes') in the next line, so that the verse is built from two words of narrowness.
Hiphil of yasha', 'to bring into open space, to deliver'. The sense of 'room' is the opposite of the tsar of the first line.

verses.translation_literal: He brings them out from darkness and deep darkness, and their fetters he tears apart.
verses.translation_dramatic: He led them out. Out of the dark, out of the thick dark where death casts its shadow, and the cords that bound them he snapped, one by one, and let them fall.
verses.directors_commentary: The prisoners of vv. 10-12 now walk out of the cell. The KJV's 'shadow of death' is the old and famous rendering of tsalmavet, and it is a mistake only in the sense that it explains too much: the Hebrew word is a single noun that most scholars read as 'deep darkness' (tsel 'shadow' + mavet, or, on the other reading, a root tsalam 'to be dark'), and the sound of 'death' in it is part of its force whichever origin one prefers. Keep both lines of darkness in the voice: choshekh, then the heavier tsalmavet. 'Brake their bands in sunder' is KJV English for the Piel of natak, 'to tear off, to rip apart'; the same word is used of pulling a seal or a cord loose (Jer 2:20). Radak glosses mosrot as the straps and shackles in which prisoners were tied, and says God arranges events so that they escape or their captors are moved to release them. This is the world of the ancient prison: a pit or a dark chamber, with leather and metal restraints.

philological_notes.note: 'Deep darkness'. Traditionally read as tsel + mavet, 'shadow of death'; many modern lexica derive it from tsalam, 'darkness'. In either reading the death-sound is heard by the audience.
Piel of natak, 'to tear away, to rip off', used for snapping cords and bonds. Metzudat Zion compares Jer 2:20 ('I broke your fetters').

verses.translation_literal: Let them give thanks to YHWH for his covenant loyalty, and for his wonders to the children of humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love, and for the wonders he has done for the sons and daughters of the human race.
verses.directors_commentary: The second refrain, the call to thanks, repeated at the end of every scene (vv. 8, 15, 21, 31). The verb is a jussive, 'let them thank', not the KJV's wistful 'Oh that men would praise', which turns a command into a sigh; the KJV supplies the 'Oh that' and the 'for'. Hebrew says thank 'to YHWH his chesed', with the object of thanks in apposition: the thanks go to God, and what they are about is his covenant loyalty. 'Goodness' is too thin for chesed, which is faithfulness to a bond. The phrase 'children of Adam' means simply human beings; it is not a limited audience. Radak says the wonders are the opening of the prisons: in the ancient city, prisoners were held behind bolted gates, so that escape took a miracle. Ibn Ezra adds that the line is for human beings so that they learn.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil jussive of yadah, 'to confess, to give thanks', publicly. It is the verb of the todah, the thank-offering, in the next verses but one; the root joins hand-gesture and confession.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast kindness. KJV's 'goodness' loses the covenant bond.

verses.translation_literal: For he broke down gates of bronze, and bars of iron he cut down.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he broke the bronze doors. He hewed through the iron bars, as one cuts down a tree.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the reason for the thanks, and the image is deliberately violent. Bronze gates and iron bars are the strongest closing a city or fortress knew; the psalmist says the LORD smashed the one and felled the other. The verb gadaʿ, 'to cut down', is the word for chopping down trees and horns (Isa 9:9 uses it of sycamores, as Metzudat Zion notes), so the iron bars fall like timber. The KJV's 'cut the bars of iron in sunder' keeps the sense but gives the line a gentle, scissors-like quality. The verse echoes Isaiah's description of Cyrus opening bronze doors (Isa 45:2), and the Hebrew nechoshet is bronze, not 'brass', which is an alloy of copper and zinc that was not common in biblical times. Rashi says the doors were locked in their faces. Metzudat David, Ibn Ezra and Meiri read the breaking as a figure for release: God arranged their escape or their pardon as though he had broken the doors.

philological_notes.note: Copper or bronze (a copper-tin alloy). The KJV's 'brass' is an anachronism: true brass was not known in this period.
'Cut down', the verb of felling trees and hewing horns. Metzudat Zion compares Isa 9:9.

verses.translation_literal: Fools, because of the way of their transgression, and because of their iniquities, they are afflicted.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fools, they were. They had gone down the road of their own rebellion, and from their own wrongdoing they were brought low, afflicted.
verses.directors_commentary: The third scene opens, and the scene changes from prisoners to the sick. The word is 'evilim, 'fools': in Proverbs the 'evil is not stupid but morally dull, a person who will not learn. The KJV puts 'fools' first as a bare label, which is right, but then 'are afflicted' loses what the Hebrew form does: yit'anu is a reflexive or passive stem, which can mean 'they bring affliction on themselves' as well as 'they are afflicted'. YLT sees this. Notice the double 'from': they suffer from the road of their transgression (a road, a habit, a course) and from their iniquities. Radak says the prisoners were not called fools because captivity comes all at once, while illness begins lightly and worsens day by day, so that only a fool fails to heed the signs. Ibn Ezra draws a parallel with the speeches of Elihu in Job, where illness is a correction. Tradition (Rashi) also attaches here the rule that a cry before the decree is sealed is answered.

philological_notes.note: Fools, in the sense of persons who are morally unteachable (the 'evil of Proverbs). Ibn Ezra says that even the wise are called fools because of their transgression.
Hithpael of 'anah, 'to afflict, to bring low': reflexive ('afflict themselves') or passive ('are afflicted'). The ambiguity is part of the verse's point.

verses.translation_literal: All food their soul loathes, and they reach to the gates of death.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every kind of food turned their stomachs. The very thought of it sickened them. And they came, step by step, to the gates of death.
verses.directors_commentary: The sickroom. The Hebrew nefesh is the word usually translated 'soul', and the KJV's 'their soul abhorreth' is literal but misleading to a modern ear: nefesh here is the throat, the appetite, the whole living self that takes in food, which is why the STEPBible gloss reads 'throat'. The sick cannot eat. Ta'ev is a strong word, 'to loathe, to abominate', the verb used of unclean things, and so the illness makes even bread an abomination. 'Gates of death' is a picture of Sheol as a walled city with gates (compare Ps 9:13; Isa 38:10): to reach its gates is to stand on the threshold. Ibn Ezra takes 'gates' to mean the grave, because with its gates shut one sees no light. Radak notes that a person in this state has already tried doctor, drink and remedy before turning to God. The KJV's 'all manner of meat' uses 'meat' in the old sense of food in general.

philological_notes.note: 'Their throat, their appetite, their very self'. Nefesh is first of all the throat and what breathes and swallows; 'soul' is a late sense.
The gates of death, the threshold of Sheol conceived as a city.

verses.translation_literal: And they cried out to YHWH in the distress to them; from their troubles he saved them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they cried out. From the very edge of the gates, they cried to the LORD, and out of those tight, pressing troubles he saved them.
verses.directors_commentary: The refrain returns word for word, as it did in v. 13. The repetition is the point: whatever the cause of the trouble and however far the person has gone, the same cry brings the same rescue. Say it the same way each time, then let the situation change the color of it. Here the cry comes from the sickbed, at the gates of death. The KJV and ASV, in a few editions, shift into the present ('they cry… he saveth'), but the Hebrew is the same wayyiqol form as in v. 13. Ibn Ezra says the psalmist includes this to teach that the guides do not help the lost, nor the jailers' friends the bound, nor the physicians the sick, nor the sailors' skill the storm-tossed: only the LORD can.

verses.translation_literal: He sends his word and heals them, and he delivers [them] from their pits.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sent his word. Only a word. No hands, no herbs, no physician bent over the bed. And they were healed. And out of the pits that had opened beneath them, he drew them free.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as quiet astonishment. In the ancient world healing was something done to the body: a physician applied oil, a poultice, a drink, a charm. Radak and Metzudat David both press the contrast: the LORD's healing is by his word alone, not by drugs or by any human act. So the actor does not rush; the word goes out, and the sick man's body answers.

The KJV's 'destructions' is the least of its guesses and the safest, but it blunts the image. The Hebrew מִשְּׁחִיתוֹתָם is built on the word for a pit (שַׁחַת), the pit of the grave. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'from the language of pit and hole', Metzudat David reads 'from the pit of the grave that was near them', and Ibn Ezra, who also allows 'destruction', ties it to the gates of Sheol of the verse before. BBE's 'underworld' catches the same pull. The sick of v.17-19 stood at death's gates; here they are pulled out of the pit beyond them. Note too the two verbs, 'heals' and 'delivers', both in the same tense: one act, seen twice.

philological_notes.note: 'His word' is the instrument of healing, not a figure for his will alone. Radak says 'his word is his will', yet sets it against the physician's work, which is done by action; the word here is sent like a messenger (ישלח), a creative command as in Ps 33:9.

From the root of 'pit' (שַׁחַת) or of 'ruin' (שחת, to destroy). The commentators split: Metzudat Zion and Meiri take 'pit' or 'net'; Radak takes it as 'their destruction', with the suffix saying that they brought it on themselves by their sin. 'Pits' keeps the grave image that the surrounding verses build.

verses.translation_literal: Let them give thanks to YHWH for his covenant loyalty, and for his wonders to the children of humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love, and for the wonders he has done for the children of men.
verses.directors_commentary: The thanksgiving refrain, as in v. 15. The same jussive and the same covenant word, but the context has changed: it is now the healed who are called to thank. Ibn Ezra says these too are obliged to give thanks. Malbim, in the next verse's note, argues that the first two sets of rescued people only thanked God for the single wonder just done for them, and that now, after a third rescue, they are to recount all of them together. As in v. 15, the KJV's 'Oh that men would praise' turns a command into a wish, and 'goodness' is a weak reading of chesed.

verses.translation_literal: And let them sacrifice sacrifices of thanksgiving, and let them recount his works with a shout of joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: And let them bring the offerings of thanks, and tell, with a ringing shout, everything he has done.
verses.directors_commentary: Only here, among the four groups, does the call to thanks add an offering. The todah, the thanksgiving sacrifice, is a shared meal offered in the temple after a deliverance (Lev 7:12-15), and the worshiper had to eat it within a day, so that the neighbors were invited and the story told. That is why the next line pairs the sacrifice with telling: the rescued must recount the works, publicly and loudly. Radak explains why the sacrifices are mentioned only for the sick: the healthy days of the recovered were long, and in the meantime they had vowed offerings, and paid them when their health returned; the prisoners, the travelers and the sailors could do the same, but it is said where it was most common. The KJV's 'declare his works with rejoicing' is serviceable; the Hebrew rinnah is a ringing shout, a cry of joy, louder than 'rejoicing'. The root zbch gives both the verb and the noun: 'sacrifice sacrifices'. The literal layer keeps that repetition.

philological_notes.note: The thanksgiving sacrifice, a communal meal consumed within a day (Lev 7:12-15). Metzudat David says it is the offering brought on account of a miracle.
A ringing cry of joy, sung or shouted aloud. Radak says they tell it among the people with a loud voice.

verses.translation_literal: Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business on many waters,
verses.translation_dramatic: And there are those who go down to the sea in ships, who work their trade on the great waters.
verses.directors_commentary: The fourth scene begins, and the psalm moves to the sailors. Israel was not a seafaring people, and the sea was a frightening world, so the picture is of other men in a trade foreign to most listeners. 'Go down to the sea' is literal: the land at the shore is higher than the water, and Ibn Ezra says 'everyone who goes to the sea goes down'. Radak offers two reasons: the shore is high, or the ship's hold is deep. The KJV's 'do business in great waters' is right in sense; the Hebrew melakhah is work, a trade or occupation, and in Radak's reading it is the working of the mast, ropes and oars. Metzudat David says it is the craft of turning the ship toward its destination. 'Many waters' (mayim rabbim) is the Hebrew phrase for the open sea or the flood, and it carries a note of danger; the KJV's 'great' is fair.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who go down to the sea'. Ibn Ezra says every one who goes to the sea goes down; Radak says it is from the height of the shore or the depth of the ship.
Work, trade, craft. Radak includes under it the mast, ropes and oars; Metzudat David the skill of steering the ship.

verses.translation_literal: They saw the works of YHWH, and his wonders in the deep.
verses.translation_dramatic: They, and no others, have seen the works of the LORD. They have seen his wonders in the deep.
verses.directors_commentary: The emphatic pronoun hemmah, 'they', opens the line: the sailors, of all people, have seen it. The KJV's 'These see' is the present sense, but the Hebrew perfect, 'they have seen', says it is something already seen and known. The deep, metsulah, is the abyss, the place where the waters are thickest and where the old stories put the sea monster and chaos. To an Israelite listener, the sea was where the gods of Canaan's neighbors fought and where Yam, the sea, was himself a god; here the psalm declares that the deep is the LORD's workshop. Radak says in the deep one sees the great fish and the heaving of the sea, and understands that God has given humans the skill to stand on planks of wood above it. Ibn Ezra says in a single moment he can shake the sea and calm it at will, which prepares the storm of the next verses.

philological_notes.note: The deep, the depth of the sea, from a root meaning to sink. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'the depth of the sea'.

verses.translation_literal: And he said, and he made stand a wind of storm, and it lifted up its waves.
verses.translation_dramatic: He spoke. And at his word a wind stood up out of nowhere, a storm-wind, and it took hold of the sea and heaved its waves high.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the sailors' strophe, and the first thing to hear is who is acting. The storm is not an accident, nor a rival god: the sentence begins 'and he said', and everything after it obeys. A Canaanite audience knew a sea-god who fought and a storm-god who rode the clouds; here the one LORD simply speaks and the wind is posted like a sentry.

The verb is וַיַּעֲמֵד, the causative of 'stand': he makes the wind stand, he appoints it to its post. KJV's 'raiseth' blurs this. Watch for the answer in v.29, where the LORD 'stands up' the storm again with a related verb, יָקֵם, from קום, 'rise'. It is not the same word, but the two belong together: one verb of standing sets the storm, another of rising turns it to a hush. The wind then lifts the waves (וַתְּרוֹמֵם, a feminine verb, so the subject is the wind), and 'its waves' are the sea's, the masculine suffix pointing back to the sea, as Ibn Ezra reads it. Play it as one slow upward motion, the whole sea rising.

philological_notes.note: Causative (hiphil) of 'stand': he causes the wind to stand, to take its post. STEPBible's 'appointed' catches the sense of commissioning. Compare יָקֵם in v.29, a related but different verb (קום).
'A wind of storm': a storm-wind, a whirlwind. The noun comes from סער 'to rage, sweep away'. It is the same word that appears for the whirlwind in which Elijah is taken up (2 Kgs 2:11).
'Its waves'. The masculine suffix cannot refer to the feminine wind or storm, so it refers to the sea (the sea of v.23, 24). Ibn Ezra says the vav of גליו returns to the sea.

verses.translation_literal: They go up [to] heavens, they go down [to] depths; their soul in evil melts away.
verses.translation_dramatic: Up they climb toward the heavens; down they plunge into the deeps. And all the while their very souls run like wax in the heat of fear.
verses.directors_commentary:
No conjunction joins 'they go up' to 'they go down'; the two clauses simply alternate, like the ship itself. Play it as a rhythm, not a list: rise, drop, rise, drop. The subject is left unnamed. Ibn Ezra allows it to be the waves or the sailors, and Radak and Metzudat David take it as the crew riding the swell, which is the plain sense.

The KJV's 'because of trouble' and 'melted' are fair, but 'their soul' (nefesh) is the whole self, throat and breath and life, and 'evil' (ra'ah) is not an abstraction but the disaster they are in. 'Melts' is the language of wax and fear: the same verb is used of hearts melting before an enemy. The sailors of the ancient Mediterranean went out in small ships, hugging coasts, and for them to be tossed between sky and the cosmic deep (tehom, the primordial water of Gen 1:2) is to be cut loose from the ordered world.

philological_notes.note: The deeps, the primeval ocean of Gen 1:2. For ancient hearers a ship dropping into the troughs approaches the abyss itself.
'melts, dissolves'. Metzudat Zion links it to 'melting, dissolving'; the fear is physical, courage liquefying.

verses.translation_literal: They reel and they sway like the drunkard, and all their wisdom is swallowed up.
verses.translation_dramatic: They lurch and they sway like drunkards on the pitching deck, and every skill they ever learned is swallowed whole by the sea.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs of motion (yachogu, yanu'u) stack up as a doublet; Radak calls it a repetition of one idea in different words, and Meiri says both mean motion of fear. The ship's crew cannot stand. They are compared to a drunk because a drunk is someone whose body no longer obeys, and the whole point is the loss of control.

The KJV's 'are at their wits' end' is a famous English idiom and it softens the Hebrew considerably. The Hebrew says their chokhmah, their 'wisdom' or professional skill, is swallowed. Chokhmah in the Bible is also the helmsman's craft (Ezek 27:8-9 speaks of the wise men of Tyre as its pilots), so this is the navigator's lore and seamanship, not only general cleverness. The verb 'swallow' is the same word used for the earth swallowing Korah; it is voracious. Radak reads it of the helmsman's art ruined that hour. Malbim adds the sea-anchor detail, that experienced sailors would try dropping iron overboard to steady the ship, which fails here.

philological_notes.note: 'their wisdom, skill': the sailors' trained craft. Radak reads it as the helmsman's skill that is ruined.
'is swallowed up'. Metzudat Zion links it to 'destroyed' (Lam 2:2); Ibn Ezra reads 'covered, unseen'. The verb is literally to gulp down.
'they reel' (a whirling, circling motion; the root of 'festival' from circling). Rashi takes it as 'break', Meiri as 'wander'.

verses.translation_literal: And they cried out to YHWH in the straits [that were] to them, and from their distresses he brings them out.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, with nothing left in their hands, they cried out to the LORD from the narrow place they were in, and out of their distress he drew them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pivot of the whole strophe and the refrain of the psalm: the same two lines recur at vv.6, 13, 19. The tone must change here, because the sailors stop doing and start crying. Their own wisdom has been swallowed in v.27, and only then do they cry.

The KJV 'in their trouble' translates tsar, which is literally 'narrow' (a tight place), and 'distresses' is metsukot, from a root meaning to be squeezed. The images are of squeezing and narrowness, so the rescue is an 'out-bringing', a word that invites the memory of the Exodus, where the same verb is used for God bringing Israel out of Egypt. The Hebrew also shifts tense: the cry is a narrative past ('they cried'), the rescue a bare imperfect ('he brings out'), as if the speaker slides from story into a timeless truth. The KJV flattens both into present ('they cry... he bringeth'). Radak asks whether the rescue is from the sea or from the distress itself; Ibn Ezra says that the sailors' whole petition was simply to be brought out.

philological_notes.note: Lit. 'in the narrow [place] to them', 'when it was narrow for them'. Tsar is the narrow strait, the same root as tsarah, distress.
'their constraints, anguishes', from a root of squeezing; used in the refrain at vv.6, 13, 19.

verses.translation_literal: He stands the storm up to a hush, and their waves were still.
verses.translation_dramatic: And again he spoke, and the storm that he had set standing he raised once more, and turned it into a hush. The wind died. The waves, so lately mountains, fell silent and lay down.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the verse answers v.25 with a related verb. There the LORD made the wind stand (עמד); here he 'stands up' (קום) the storm, and this time it rises into a hush. The two verbs are not the same, but both are verbs of standing, and the answer is meant to be heard. Radak and Metzudat David read יָקֵם as 'returns', that is, the storm he raised he brings back to stillness; the literal 'stands the storm up' holds both senses, because the same word that sets it can end it.

The KJV's 'He maketh the storm a calm' is clear and fair, but flattens two things. First, דְּמָמָה is not just calm but a hush, the very word of the 'sound of a thin silence' to Elijah (1 Kgs 19:12), as Metzudat Zion notes; it is silence heard after noise. Second, the waves 'were still' (וַיֶּחֱשׁוּ) with the verb of keeping quiet, as in Eccl 3:7 'a time to be silent': the waves had a voice, and now they have none. And the suffix: v.25 said 'its waves', here it is 'their waves', which the KJV smooths to 'thereof'. Meiri says they are the sailors' waves, the ones that rose against them. Play it as a held breath let go.

philological_notes.note: From קום, 'to rise, stand'; here causative, 'make stand up'. It answers v.25's וַיַּעֲמֵד (עמד) with a related verb of standing. Radak records the view that it means 'returns' (ישוב) and then gives the plain sense, that the storm he had raised he turns into a hush.
A hush, a stillness after sound; the word of 1 Kgs 19:12, 'a voice of thin silence'. It is silence heard, not mere absence.
'Were quiet, kept silent', as in Eccl 3:7 ('a time to be silent'). Ibn Ezra notes that, since waves have a sound, silence is the figure for their ceasing, the opposite of 'lifted up' in v.25.

verses.translation_literal: And they rejoice because they are quiet, and he leads them to the territory of their desire.
verses.translation_dramatic: And joy comes over them, because the sea has gone quiet; and he leads them on, to the shore their hearts were set upon.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sailors rejoice at silence, which is the strangest joy: after the roar of the storm, the greatest gift is quiet. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say the subject of 'they are quiet' is the waves; the Hebrew's third plural, ambiguous between waves and men, lets both resonate.

The word the KJV renders 'haven', machoz, is rare and means 'territory, border, region' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all gloss it so). Later translators took it as 'harbor' from the context of a ship; this is a reasonable guess, but not the Hebrew word's plain meaning. 'The desired haven' is also KJV's rhetorical lift: the Hebrew says 'their desire', chefets, their wish or aim, which is the destination they set out for before the storm. The verb 'led' (nachah) is the shepherd's verb of guiding, as in Exodus 13:17, and it recasts the ship's pilot as a guided flock.

philological_notes.note: 'territory, district'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra give it the sense of 'boundary'; Radak 'the border of their desire'. 'Haven' is an inference from context, not the word's sense.
'and he led them': the verb of guidance, used of God leading Israel (Exod 13:17). Rashi glosses it 'drove, led them'.

verses.translation_literal: Let them give thanks to YHWH [for] his loyal love, and [for] his wonders to the sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them give thanks to the LORD for his steadfast love, and for his wonders done for the children of humankind.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the refrain (see vv.8, 15, 21) and it should be spoken as a cry, not a conclusion. The tone shifts from narrated rescue to a summons: the sailors are safe, and now the whole audience is called to thank.

The KJV 'Oh that men would praise the Lord for his goodness' makes a wistful exclamation of a plain jussive and trades chesed (covenant loyalty, steadfast love, the commitment God keeps) for the thin 'goodness'. 'For his goodness' also hides that Hebrew has no 'for': 'his chesed and his wonders' are what is thanked. The verb is hodu, 'confess, acknowledge, give thanks', the root of todah, thank-offering. Ibn Ezra glosses chesed as the rescue and the wonders as what happened in the depths. 'Sons of Adam' is simply humankind; the KJV 'children of men' keeps the idiom.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love; the central attribute of God in the psalm. Ibn Ezra reads it here as the rescue itself.
Hiphil jussive: 'let them give thanks, acknowledge'. It is the root of todah, the thank-offering, and the wording of the psalm's opening call (Ps 107:1).

verses.translation_literal: And let them exalt him in the assembly of [the] people, and in the seat of [the] elders let them praise him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them lift him high before the gathered people, and in the council seat of the elders let their praise ring out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The thanks must be public. Two venues are named: the qahal 'am, the whole people's gathering, and the moshav zeqenim, the 'seat' or sitting of the elders, the city-gate court where law was judged (cf. Ruth 4:1-2, where Boaz sits in the gate with ten elders). Play the contrast: the crowd and the council, the noisy and the formal.

The KJV's 'Let them exalt him also' inserts an 'also' that is not in the Hebrew, and 'assembly of the elders' is softer than 'seat', which names a sitting body. The verb 'exalt' (romem) is the same root as 'lifted up' in v.25: the waves were lifted by the storm, now God is lifted by his people's praise. The rabbis took the verse to require that thanks for rescue be said before ten and two of them scholars (Rashi on this verse, citing b. Berakhot 54b and Bava Batra 15a), which is a later derivation. Ibn Ezra says the verse repeats the call because most people never saw the sea.

philological_notes.note: Polel of 'be high': 'let them exalt him'. It is the root of תְּרוֹמֵם 'it lifted up' in v.25, so the lifting of the waves is answered by the lifting of God.
'seat of the elders', the sitting of the elders' council, often at the city gate. Rashi cites the rabbinic rule to give thanks before ten and two scholars.

verses.translation_literal: He makes rivers into a wilderness, and springs of water into thirsty ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: He turns rivers into wilderness, and the places where water wells up into parched and thirsting earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm's tone turns abruptly from the sea to the land and from individuals to whole territories. The refrain is gone; now a wisdom-poem on God's power to reverse landscapes. Play it as a slow, grave reversal after the crowd's noise.

The verse has two parallel lines and the second adds an image: 'springs' (motsa'ei mayim, 'places where water comes out') and 'thirst' (tsima'on, a word for dry land that also means thirst itself). The KJV 'dry ground' and 'watersprings' are accurate but lose the personification: the land is thirsty. 'Rivers' (neharot) in the Near East were life itself, the Nile, the Tigris, the Euphrates, and a river turned into wilderness is a civilization's end. Radak and Meiri tie the reversal to the sins of the inhabitants; Rashi reads it as turning inhabited places to ruin.

philological_notes.note: 'thirsty land', literally 'thirstiness': a place of thirst, a rare noun.
'outgoings of water', the springs; Ibn Ezra glosses the term as 'springs' (ma'yanim).

verses.translation_literal: A land of fruit into saltness, from the evil of those who dwell in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: A land that bore fruit he turns to salt, for the wickedness of the people who live upon it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse ends on a moral: the judgment is not random. 'From the evil of those who dwell in it' gives the reason; Ibn Ezra says the Lord does not act for nothing, and Metzudat David that the land's ruin is the people's due.

The KJV 'barrenness' is a wide gloss. The Hebrew is melechah, 'saltness', a salt waste. In the ancient Near East, salting a land was a curse and a sign of ruin: Sodom and the Dead Sea region are the picture in the Targum, and Deuteronomy 29:23 describes Sodom's ruin as 'brimstone and salt'; Judges 9:45 has Abimelech sow a razed city with salt. The KJV's 'barrenness' hides that image. The Hebrew also says 'land of fruit', a fruit-land, a place defined by its yield, which makes the reversal sharper.

philological_notes.note: 'into saltiness, a salt waste'. Rashi: a land of salt that bears no fruit. The image of salted land is a curse of ruin (Judg 9:45; Deut 29:23).
'from the evil of': the same ra'ah that in v.26 was the sailors' disaster. Here it is the inhabitants' wrongdoing that causes ruin.

verses.translation_literal: He makes a wilderness into a pool of water, and a land of dryness into springs of water.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he turns the wilderness into a pool of water, and the bone-dry land into springs that bubble up.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reversal now runs the other way, and the voice should brighten. The verse mirrors v.33 almost word for word, with the nouns swapped: 'rivers into wilderness' becomes 'wilderness into a pool'. The poem is built to show that the same God holds both directions.

The KJV 'standing water' translates agam, a marsh or pool, a shallow lake of reeds; the Hebrew is a word for a gathering of water. 'Dry ground' here is 'a land of tsiyah', the driest of dry lands, and Malbim notes that it is even drier than midbar, 'wilderness', so the miracle is greater. In the arid Near East, a spring in the desert was the difference between a camp and a city. Radak and Meiri tie this half to the people God chooses; Rashi reads it as a ruined settlement restored.

philological_notes.note: 'pool, marsh, reedy pond'. Metzudat Zion: a place where water gathers. KJV's 'standing water' is right.
'dry land, parched ground'. Malbim treats it as drier than 'wilderness'; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'desolation'.

verses.translation_literal: And he causes the hungry to dwell there, and they establish a city of dwelling.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there he settles the hungry, and they raise up a city to live in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb shifts: 'he causes to dwell' (God, singular) and then 'they establish' (the people, plural). God gives the place; the hungry build the city. Play the quiet pride in that division of labour.

The KJV 'he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city' turns the second clause into a purpose, 'that they may', which the Hebrew does not have: the Hebrew is two plain clauses joined by 'and', the settling and the founding. The 'hungry' (re'evim) are the displaced, the refugees, those who had no land; Radak says they came 'from here and there' to this place. The word 'city of dwelling' (ir moshav) is an inhabited city, not a camp: the same moshav as in v.32's 'seat of elders', suggesting the council of elders will sit here. The verb 'establish' (konenu) is the verb used for founding and for God establishing the earth, so the rescued town is a small creation.

philological_notes.note: 'the hungry': the displaced poor who find nothing to eat elsewhere. Radak: those who had been hungry in another place and came to settle here.
Polel of 'be firm': 'they established, set firmly'. The verb of founding a city or a throne.

verses.translation_literal: And they sowed fields, and they planted vineyards, and they made fruit of produce.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the work began: they scattered seed across the fields, they pressed young vines into the earth, row on patient row, and the land gave back what they had put into it, fruit and harvest.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as the quiet turn from rescue to ordinary life. The people who were dying in the desert wasteland (vv. 4-9 and v. 35) are now ordinary farmers, and the rhythm of the verse is the rhythm of work: three short clauses, each opening with 'and they'. Sowing a field and planting a vineyard are two very different bets. Grain gives a return within a season, but a vine takes about three years before it bears, so anyone who plants vineyards is a person who expects to still be there. That is the whole point of the verse, security measured in time.

The KJV turns the verbs into purpose ('which may yield fruits of increase'), but the Hebrew has no 'may'. It is a plain sequence: they sowed, they planted, they made. The people are the ones doing the producing here, and the verse says it as a flat fact of their settled life, a point Radak underlines by reading the result as success. The closing pair 'fruit of produce' (pĕrî tĕvuʾāh) piles up two near-synonyms. Metzudat David reads them as a division: vineyards give the fruit and fields give the grain, and Radak says it is a doubling of one idea in different words.

philological_notes.note: A construct pair, literally 'fruit of produce'. Tĕvuʾāh is from the root 'to come in': what comes in at harvest. The two words are close in meaning; Radak calls it a doubling of one idea in different words, Metzudat David splits it between vineyard fruit and field grain.

verses.translation_literal: And he blessed them, and they multiplied exceedingly, and their cattle he did not make few.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he blessed them. They grew, and grew again, past all counting, and their herds he never let thin: the folds stayed full, the pastures stayed loud.
verses.directors_commentary:
The subject has quietly changed. In v. 37 the people were the actors; now it is 'he', God, and the verb is 'blessed'. In the ancient world blessing is not a feeling but a power, the force that makes things fertile, and the proof is on the ground: more children and fuller herds. Radak splits it exactly so, finding the blessing in wealth, in children (the 'multiplying') and in livestock that never miscarry, and Meiri agrees on the livestock.

The last clause is a litotes: 'their cattle he did not make few'. Wealth in a herding economy was counted in animals, and a bad winter could wipe a family out, so 'not make few' says more than it first seems. The KJV's 'suffereth not their cattle to decrease' has God merely allowing it. The Hebrew verb is causative (yamʿît), and the sentence says he does not cause them to become few, so the agency remains his. Note too the sound play with the verse that follows: the verb 'make few' (māʿaṭ) comes back as the first word of v. 39.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of the root for 'few, small'. The next verse opens with the same root in the plain stem ('they became few'), so the blessing of v. 38 is undone by its own word in v. 39.

verses.translation_literal: And they became few, and they were bowed down, from the restraint of calamity and sorrow.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then they dwindled. Fewer, and fewer, and the survivors bent low, pressed under the crushing weight of evil days and sorrow.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the second half of the psalm, and the sharpest turn in it. The opening verb is the exact root of the end of v. 38 ('he did not make few'), now with the people as subject: 'and they became few'. The prosperity just described is not guaranteed. The Hebrew gives no 'again' and no 'when'; the KJV's 'Again' is added, and its 'through oppression, affliction, and sorrow' smooths a hard string of nouns into an even list. Say the verse flatly, with no reason given.

The verb 'were bowed down' (shāḥaḥ) is a picture of the body: stooped, bent double. Radak reads it as the reverse of walking upright (qomemiyyut, Lev 26:13). The word oṣer is the hard one. It comes from the root 'to hold back, restrain', and Radak and Meiri take it as the control of a ruler who holds a people under him, the sense it has in Judg 18:7. KJV 'oppression' is therefore close, and YLT 'restraint' is closer to the root. The three losses, restraint, calamity and sorrow, run from a political cause through bodily harm to inner grief, which is how Radak divides the last two (the body and wealth, then the heart).

philological_notes.note: To be bowed or brought low, a body bent under a load. Metzudat Zion ties it to the 'helpers of Rahab' who stoop beneath him in Job 9:13; Radak sets it against the upright walk of the free.

From the root 'to hold back, restrain': a restraint or authority imposed from outside. Radak reads it as the rule of others over them; Metzudat Zion links it to 'let us detain you' in Judg 13:15. Ibn Ezra also offers a reading from 'womb', which is a less likely derivation.

verses.translation_literal: Pouring contempt on nobles, and he made them wander in a waste, no way.
verses.translation_dramatic: He pours out contempt upon the great, and sends them stumbling through an emptiness with no road, no path, no way at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar here has a lurch in it that the KJV irons out. The first verb is a participle, 'pouring', with no stated subject, and then the sentence jumps into a narrative past: 'and he made them wander'. Speak it as a flash from the hand of the one who holds all of this, God pouring out rather than anyone else. The image of pouring is physical and wet. Contempt is a liquid in this verse, tipped from a jug over the heads of the high and mighty, the way a libation or a wrath is poured. The nobles (nĕdîvîm) are men of means, 'givers', so called because their rank was shown by generosity; Metzudat Zion calls them 'lords with gifts to give'.

Then the word tohu: the same word as 'formless and empty' in Gen 1:2. The KJV's 'wilderness, where there is no way' replaces it with a plain desert. It is stronger than that: it is the chaos before creation, a nothing with no marked road. Meiri says it is a place so empty even a child could not get lost there, yet the great are lost in it. A power whose whole career is built on knowing the route is reduced to feeling its way across empty ground.

philological_notes.note: 'Waste, formlessness, nothing'. It is the word of Gen 1:2 and of the trackless desert of Deut 32:10, and here it marks a place with no road. Meiri reads it as 'anything that is nothing'.
Nobles, from the root 'to give willingly': those whose rank shows in giving. Radak: the rich and honoured, who were called nĕdîvîm.

verses.translation_literal: And he set the needy on high from affliction, and he made families like the flock.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the poor man he lifts out of his misery and sets high, beyond the reach of it, and gives him families as many as a flock, spreading across the hills.
verses.directors_commentary:
The great reversal, and it needs a change of voice: after four verses of descent, lift. The verb 'set on high' (vayĕsaggēv) is from the root for a high place of safety, the same root as the 'refuge' (miśgāv) that the Psalms use for God. The poor man is not simply helped; he is placed where he cannot be reached. 'From affliction' is a movement, 'out of', and the KJV 'setteth ... from' is nearly right but stiff.

The last image is the one to play. Families 'like the flock' is a statement about fertility and security at once: a flock grows quickly, spreads and is looked after, and a man of means was one who owned many sheep. Rashi reads it as the poor man's descendants becoming as many as a flock; Radak adds that the sheep were chosen because they outnumber other animals, and that the families have no barren and no bereaved. The KJV 'maketh him families' adds a 'him' that the Hebrew does not have, though the sense is the same. The text makes the poor man, not the nobles of v. 40, the one who gets a future.

philological_notes.note: To set on a height out of reach. The related noun is the 'stronghold' (miśgāv) that the Psalter uses for God as refuge; Radak sets this verb against the 'bowed down' of v. 39.
The needy or destitute man, one who is reduced to begging. Here it is paired with ʿŏnî, 'affliction', in a single clause.

verses.translation_literal: The upright see and they rejoice, and all unrighteousness has shut its mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: The upright see it, and they are glad. And all wrongdoing shuts its mouth, and has not a word left to say.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two audiences, two reactions, and the verse sets them side by side. The upright watch and rejoice; injustice, personified, falls silent. Make the second half physical: injustice is a person with a mouth, and the mouth snaps shut. The verb qāfaṣ is a clamping, as of a fist (Deut 15:7, 'you shall not shut your hand'; Rashi cites that verse and Metzudat Zion cites Ps 77:10 for the same verb).

The KJV 'shall see it' supplies an object and a future that the Hebrew lacks; the verbs are a plain imperfect and a perfect, so the scene is open-ended, a standing truth rather than a prediction. Its 'the righteous' also blurs the word: yĕshārîm are the 'straight' or 'level', people whose lives run along a plumb line, and the pairing with ʿawlāh, 'crookedness, unfairness', is a contrast of straight against bent. Meiri is careful on one point that a director should keep: the upright do not gloat over the fall of others; their joy is that the noise of violence has stopped. Ibn Ezra adds that they rejoice because they now expect good for themselves, like the poor man.

philological_notes.note: 'Shut her mouth', a clamping closed. The same verb is used of a closed fist in Deut 15:7. Injustice here is a speaker who has no answer left.

verses.translation_literal: Who is wise, and let him keep these, and let them consider the loyal acts of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who is wise? Let that one keep these things close, and weigh them well, and let them all see how deep the steadfast love of the LORD runs.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a question aimed at the room. This is the language of the wisdom teachers: 'Who is wise?' is not a request for information, it is a challenge, as in Hos 14:10. Deliver it slowly, to the audience, and then wait. The KJV makes it a sentence of promise ('Whoso is wise ... shall understand'); the Hebrew has two jussives, 'let him keep', 'let them consider', which are an invitation, not a forecast. The ASV and BBE come closer.

The small grammatical shift matters. 'Let him keep' is singular, one wise person; 'let them consider' is plural. The one becomes a community of readers, which is how a psalm for the temple crowd turns into a lesson for everyone. 'These things' (ʾēlleh) are the whole chain of reversals just described, and Radak and Malbim both read the verse as a conclusion drawn from them: God raises and lowers, enriches and impoverishes, and the wise person sees it is not chance. The last word is the one the whole psalm has been rehearsing since v. 1: ḥesed, covenant loyalty, here in the plural, ḥasdê YHWH, 'the loyal acts of the LORD'. The KJV 'lovingkindness' is a Coverdale coinage that makes the word soft. It is a duty kept under an oath, and it is always shown in deeds.

philological_notes.note: A plural: not one trait of God but his repeated acts of covenant loyalty. The psalm opened with the same word (v. 1) and refrains on it (vv. 8, 15, 21, 31).
Jussive: 'let him keep'. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'lay these things up in his heart'; Radak and Meiri likewise take 'keep' as keeping in mind, not keeping a rule.
